passages.where: The father tells the slacker to watch the ant, which with no overseer prepares its food in summer and gathers at harvest. The site's note on the chapter says he urges the lazy to learn from it. Putting something by in the good season is presented as ordinary wisdom, not a lack of faith.

Precious treasure and oil are kept in the house of the wise, but a foolish man consumes them. The site's note on the chapter says it warns against haste, pleasure and greed, and verse 17 says the one who loves pleasure will become poor. The difference between the two houses is not income but what happens to it.

Dishonest wealth dwindles, but what is earned through hard work is multiplied. The site's note on the chapter says it sets wealth gained slowly beside wealth gained dishonestly, and takes the long view of an inheritance left to grandchildren. Proverbs trusts the slow, honest way over the quick win.

Joseph advises Pharaoh to store a fifth of the harvest in the years of plenty as a reserve for the years of famine. The site's plain note says Joseph trusted God's word and still made a careful plan, and asks whether you treat trusting God and planning ahead as opposites. It asks what wise preparation, not worry, would look like in your home this year.

Know the state of your flocks and pay attention to your herds, for riches are not forever. The site's note on the chapter calls this a short poem urging the reader to know the condition of what he has, because wealth and even crowns do not last, while faithful work provides for a household. In modern terms it is close to knowing where the money goes.

Cast your bread on the waters, the Teacher says, and divide your portion among seven or eight, for you do not know what disaster may come. The site's note on the chapter says he urges bold and generous action in the face of an uncertain future, because no one knows which effort will succeed. Uncertainty is a reason for wide, open-handed prudence, not for paralysis.

After feeding the crowd, Jesus tells his disciples to gather the leftover pieces so that nothing will be wasted. The site's note says only John records the order, and that the care not to waste treats God's gift as precious rather than cheap. Abundance did not make waste acceptable.

When a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus, some call it waste and say it could have been sold for the poor, and Jesus calls it a beautiful deed. The site's note says he is not setting devotion against care for the poor, which he assumes his followers will keep up. The plain note adds that people who say think of the poor are not always thinking of the poor; careful money is not the same as a closed hand.

Jesus says whoever is faithful with very little will be faithful with much, and asks who will trust with true riches someone unfaithful with worldly wealth. The site's note says the verses do not despise money but relativize it, calling it very little and another's. The plain note asks you to look at how you used money last week, and whom it served.

Within days the younger son turns everything into cash, goes to a distant country and squanders it in wild living. The site's note says Luke says only that he lived wastefully, and that the loss of the property followed the loss of the relationship with his father. Spending that runs away from something is a different thing from spending that enjoys a gift.

misread.taken: Do not worry about tomorrow is used to say that saving, insurance or planning for the future shows a lack of faith, since a believer should simply trust God for each day.
misread.says: The site's note on the passage says the disciples are not told to stop working: the birds do not farm, but humans do. It says verse 34 limits the load to one day at a time and that faith does not deny trouble but declines to borrow tomorrow's, and that the promise is food and clothes, not wealth. Joseph, the plain note on Genesis 41 says, trusted God's word and still made a careful plan; what Jesus forbids is the anxious striving, not the barn.

whole: Most people do not think of their bank statement as a spiritual document, but it is one of the most honest records of a life. Some people cannot save at all: the money is gone before the month is, on bills and rent and children, and the advice to put something by sounds like a joke. Others can save and cannot stop: they check the balance like a pulse, feel guilty at every purchase, and hold back from generosity because there might never be enough. Many live somewhere between, spending on impulse, borrowing to cover it, and feeling both the pleasure of the buy and the weight of the card.

Scripture does not treat money as dirty, and it does not treat it as neutral. It praises the ant that gathers in summer and Joseph who stored grain in the good years, and it warns that the lover of pleasure becomes poor and that dishonest gain dwindles. It also tells the story of a son who turned everything into cash and squandered it, and of a man who built bigger barns and spoke only to himself. Beneath both overspending and hoarding the Bible sees the same thing, a heart looking to money for what only God can give: escape and comfort in the one case, security and control in the other. The note on Luke 16 says money is very little and another's, and the trouble starts when we treat it as much and our own.

So the Bible's wisdom is ordinary and steady. Know the state of your flocks: know what comes in and what goes out. Gather little by little, honestly, rather than chasing the quick win. Put something by in the good season, as Joseph did, without letting the saving become a god. Waste nothing that can be used, as Jesus had the leftovers gathered, and still be capable of a beautiful extravagance where love calls for it. Spread what you have wisely, since no one knows the future. Be faithful with the little, because the little shows what we would do with much. For debts, bills and real decisions about what to do next, talk to someone qualified to advise you; the Bible gives the heart, and good counsel helps with the numbers.

The hope Scripture gives is that the LORD is a portion no market can take away. The psalmist says his boundary lines have fallen in pleasant places, and he is speaking of God before he is speaking of land. A person who knows that has no need to spend in order to feel alive, or to hoard in order to feel safe. They can save without fear, spend without guilt, and give without counting every coin, because what they have was never theirs to begin with and the one who gave it is not finished giving.
sit: If someone read your last month's spending, what would they say you love, and what would you want them to see?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note asks what your portion is, the thing you count on to make life good, and asks you to say honestly what you would most hate to lose. Pray these lines as a way of naming God as that portion.
